judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the homepage masthead, an image of the words "THE IRISH TIMES" (I checked the crop and the screenshot). It is not in a link and is not hidden, and its alt is "Masthead logo". That alt names what kind of image it is but not what it says, so a screen reader user hears "Masthead logo" and never the publication's name. Strictly, the image does show a masthead logo, so the finding's wording ("describes something the image does not show") is a little off. The real defect is that the alt is generic and does not convey the logo's text (alt="The Irish Times" would). If the masthead were treated as decorative, a non-empty alt would instead fail F39. Either way 1.1.1 fails. The live page still has the same alt.

The red dot is a separate pseudo-element and does not change the text's contrast. This is a functional section link, not incidental text or a logotype, so 1.4.3 fails.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the live-blog timeline entry link ("1 hour ago / The storm set to hit Ireland's west coast..."). The <a> wraps an <article> that holds the time and paragraph. In the snapshot, Chrome's accessibility tree gives the link role link and name "": Chromium does not take a name from the contents of an article descendant, and the link has no aria-label or title. So when a screen reader user tabs to this focusable link, or lists the links, it is announced only as "link", and its name is not programmatically determinable in the engine the page was tested in. That fails 4.1.2, and 2.4.4 as well. Some auditors might call this a browser quirk, since AccName 1.2 recursion would include the text. But the name the platform actually exposes is empty, and the fix is trivial. The live page has changed since the run: it no longer shows the live-blog lead, so I judged from the snapshot.
